title: Christianity and Secularism
welcome_lead: Walk the streets of secularising Europe with Nietzsche, Freud, and Dawkins, and meet Christian thinkers who took up the challenge.
meta_desc: A-Level Edexcel Religious Studies adventure on Christianity and secular challenges: Nietzsche, Freud, Dawkins, and Christian responses.
final_note: You have engaged the major secular critiques of religion and key Christian replies.

concepts.def: The sociological claim that modernity inevitably reduces religion's social significance.
Nietzsche's image, in The Gay Science section 125, for the collapse of belief in the Christian God in Western culture.
Feuerbach's view that God is humanity's projected ideal self.
Freud's term for religion in The Future of an Illusion: wish-fulfilment rooted in childhood need.
The early-2000s movement of Dawkins, Dennett, Harris and Hitchens emphasising scientific naturalism.
Jurgen Habermas's diagnosis of contemporary society as one in which religion has returned to public life.

walkthroughs.body_html: Feuerbach's Essence of Christianity (1841) argued that theology is anthropology: God is humanity's projection. Marx famously called religion 'the opium of the people' in his 1844 introduction to Hegel's Philosophy of Right - both consolation and ideology masking exploitation. Nietzsche, in The Gay Science (1882) section 125, narrated the madman's proclamation that 'God is dead... and we have killed him'.

Freud's The Future of an Illusion (1927) and Civilization and its Discontents (1930) treated religion as wish-fulfilment, projecting paternal authority onto the cosmos. Richard Dawkins's The God Delusion (2006), Daniel Dennett's Breaking the Spell, Sam Harris's The End of Faith, and Christopher Hitchens's God Is Not Great mounted the New Atheist polemic.

Karl Barth's Church Dogmatics distinguishes religion (human projection) from revelation, granting Feuerbach his critique of religion while preserving the Word of God. Alister McGrath replies to Dawkins in The Dawkins Delusion? (2007). Charles Taylor's A Secular Age (2007) charts a more nuanced narrative than simple decline. Habermas advocates dialogue between secular and religious citizens.
